items.text: A fake API with the real protocol makes tests free and repeatable
One function decides: real client or offline client
Every call is costed; a budget check runs before each call
Errors are mapped once; fallbacks handle refusals

captions.text: Project time.
Over two lessons you'll build the AI Study Assistant: a command line tool that
explains programming concepts, writes quizzes as validated JSON, and chats with
memory, while tracking every cent it spends.
Everything from this module appears in it.
The explain command streams an explanation of any topic, at a beginner,
intermediate, or advanced level.
The quiz command generates multiple-choice questions as validated JSON, which you
can save and grade.
The chat command holds a conversation with history, trimmed to a token budget.
Every call reports its tokens and cost, and a budget stops runaway spending.
And it has clear errors, automatic retries, and an offline mode, so the tests never
need a key or the network.
The command line handles arguments and printing, and calls the assistant, which
holds the logic for explaining, quizzing, and chatting.
Prompts live in their own module, so you can improve them without touching the code.
And models holds the quiz schema.
Pricing calculates costs and enforces the budget.
And client builds the SDK client: a real one when your key is set, or the same SDK
pointed at the offline fake API when it isn't.
Nothing else in the program knows the difference.
Let's start with the piece that makes testing possible: the fake API.
It's a class whose objects can be called like a function, once per HTTP request.
A list of planned failures lets tests and demos make it return a four twenty-nine or
a five hundred on purpose.
Each call receives the real HTTP request the SDK built, and parses its JSON body.
It records the body, so tests can check exactly what was sent, and it answers token
counting requests with a rough estimate.
Then it prepares a placeholder reply, applies any planned failure or refusal, cuts
the reply at max tokens just like the real API, and returns either a normal JSON
message or a stream of server-sent events.
Because the responses have the same shape as the real API's, the SDK can't tell the
difference.
That means our tests exercise the real SDK code.
With a key, we create a normal client.
The SDK reads the key from the environment, so it never appears in our code.
We pass the retry count and a sixty-second timeout.
Without a key, we print a clear offline notice, and give the same SDK an HTTP client
whose transport is our fake API instead of the network.
Settings come from environment variables, as in Module 1.
If there's no key, we switch to offline mode automatically.
The model defaults to Claude Opus 5.5, and the budget to fifty cents.
The price table holds dollars per million input and output tokens, for each model.
Cost u s d is the formula from lesson five.
An unknown model raises an error rather than silently costing zero.
The cost tracker adds up spending.
Its check method runs before every call, and raises budget exceeded once the budget
is used up.
That's your protection against a runaway loop.
And add records the cost of each finished call.
An Answer bundles everything we learn from a call: the text, the stop reason, the
tokens, and the cost.
Truncated is true when the reply hit max tokens.
Friendly errors is a context manager that catches SDK exceptions, most specific
first, and turns each into one clear message.
It's lesson five's error table, written once and reused by every call.
Next, fallbacks.
If the model declines a request, the API can re-run it on another model
automatically.
We opt in with this beta flag.
And base builds the arguments every request shares: the model, the beta flag, and
fallbacks set to default, so the API chooses a suitable fallback model for us.
Answer turns a response into an Answer.
It records the cost first, because even a declined request is billed, then checks
for a refusal, and only then joins the text blocks.
Explain checks the budget first, then fills in the request template from prompts dot
py.
It opens a stream, inside friendly errors, using the shared arguments, the tutor
system prompt, and low effort, which is plenty for explanations.
Each piece of text is passed to an on text callback as it arrives, so the assistant
doesn't know or care whether it's printed, shown in a web page, or collected by a
test.
Then the final message becomes an Answer.
Let's run it.
The offline notice comes first, then the streamed placeholder, then a footer with
the model, tokens, cost, and stop reason, and finally the session total against the
budget.
With a tiny max tokens, the reply is cut off, and the tool warns you instead of
pretending everything is fine.
And with a budget of zero, it refuses before sending anything, with a one-line
explanation.
A fake API that speaks the real protocol makes tests free and repeatable.
One function decides between the real and the offline client.
Every call is costed, and a budget check runs before each one.
Errors are mapped once, in one place, and fallbacks handle refusals.
In part two: quizzes as structured output, chat with history, the full demo, the
tests, and the module quiz.
